title: Commands that keep running
lead: Today a command the assistant runs is killed after 10 minutes, and nothing can outlive a call — no dev servers, no long builds. The design you approved in chat: the assistant can run a command in the background, you see it live on its card with a Stop button, and the assistant is told when it finishes. These are the card's five states, built in the design sandbox with invented output. Five Yes/No steps.

steps.path: Chat → the assistant starts a command in the background
steps.headline: A background command shows a live status strip with a Stop button, and its output keeps updating while you chat.
steps.changed: The card header gains “· in the background” and a spinner. Below the command sits a strip: “Running in the background · 2m 18s” with the one action that ends it — Stop. Under that, the last lines of output (“Live output”), then the path of the full log file.
steps.measured: Strip 44 px tall; output box shows up to 20 lines
steps.notice: Stop ends the command and everything it launched, so stopping a dev server really stops the server. The timer ticks every second. You can keep chatting; the assistant keeps working.
steps.risk: The live output only refreshes when new lines arrive — a command that prints nothing looks frozen even when it is working (the ticking timer is the sign of life).

steps.path: Chat → a normal command hits its time limit
steps.headline: A command that hits its time limit is moved to the background instead of being killed, and the strip says so.
steps.changed: Same strip, different second line: “Hit its time limit and kept running in the background — you'll be told when it finishes.” No new button.
steps.notice: A 12-minute build now simply finishes. The 10-minute hard cap is gone; the assistant is told at the 2-minute mark that the command moved, and carries on.
steps.risk: A command that is genuinely stuck (waiting for input it will never get) now sits in the background instead of dying — Stop is the way out, and the timer makes the wait visible.

steps.headline: When it finishes, the strip is replaced by a green “Exit 0 · 11m 42s” chip and the card reads like any finished command.
steps.changed: The header drops “· in the background” and shows the tick. Two chips at the top: “Background” and “Exit 0 · 11m 42s” (green for exit 0). Output and the log path stay.
steps.notice: The assistant is told at its next pause — exit code, the last lines, the log path — and picks the work back up. Nothing lands mid-sentence.
steps.risk: Chips are uppercase small text, the app's existing chip style; a long elapsed time (“1h 12m”) still fits.

steps.headline: A non-zero exit shows a red “Exit 1” chip and the header's cross, with the failing output right there.
steps.changed: Same layout as a success; the exit chip turns red and the header icon is the failure cross. The last lines of output usually carry the reason.
steps.notice: The assistant sees the same exit code and lines, so it can act on the failure without you relaying it.
steps.risk: Exit code alone is the signal — a command that prints “error” but exits 0 shows green, as it would in a terminal.

steps.path: Chat → you close the conversation with a command still running
steps.headline: A command that was stopped says who stopped it and after how long — never a mystery.
steps.changed: An amber chip names the reason — “Stopped by you”, “Stopped by the assistant”, “Stopped when the conversation closed”, or “Stopped when the app quit” — plus “after 40m”. The header shows the stopped mark and a STOPPED tag, same as a stopped helper.
steps.notice: Closing a conversation or quitting the app stops what it started, and the card records that. Switching conversations does not stop anything.
steps.risk: If the app crashes (not quits), nothing gets the chance to stop the command or write this chip — the command keeps running and the card shows the last state it knew.
